The Mink frog reaches an ultimate female snout-vent length of 7.6 centimeters [Li = 7.6 centimeters], a measurement derived from extensive field sampling across its northern range. Upon eclosion from the jelly-coated egg, the newly emerged aquatic larva possesses a wet weight at birth of 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], reflecting a modest initial mass based on the egg diameter of roughly two millimeters. This endotrophic tadpole undergoes a period of yolk absorption before transitioning to exogenous feeding, entering a phase of rapid growth as a free-swimming larva. The species exhibits delayed sexual maturation; under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 15 °C [T = 15 °C], females attain sexual maturity approximately 365 days after birth [tp = approximately 365 days after birth], at which point their snout-vent length measures 6.8 centimeters [Lp = 6.8 centimeters]. This developmental timeline is consistent with the relatively slow pace of life history observed in northern ranid frogs, where a prolonged growing season is curtailed by harsh winter conditions.

Males follow a slightly different developmental trajectory, reaching puberty at a smaller body size of 5.9 centimeters [Lp = 5.9 centimeters] SVL. The time since birth at puberty for males under the same stable thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] is also 365 days since birth [tp = 365 days since birth], indicating that the primary sex difference in the onset of reproductive maturity is somatic rather than chronological. The gravid female amphibian, upon reaching reproductive activation, can produce a substantial number of offspring in a single reproductive event. Field records from northern populations indicate that fecundity per clutch ranges from 500 to 4000 eggs [N_R_i = per clutch ranges from 500 to 4000 eggs], and females typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This annual reproductive output is characteristic of a bet-hedging strategy common among amphibians inhabiting ephemeral or unpredictable boreal wetlands.

Adult female body mass reaches an ultimate wet weight of 48.7 grams [Wwi = 48.7 grams], a value derived from allometric scaling relationships based on the 7.6 centimeter maximum SVL. This represents a substantial increase from the 22.9 grams recorded for females at a smaller reference size of 5.91 centimeters. The post-metamorphic juvenile froglet enters a period of sustained somatic growth, gradually accumulating the body condition necessary to survive the long winter dormancy. The maximum lifespan recorded in wild populations is approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years], a figure observed in individuals maintained at a mean environmental temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] during the active season. This longevity is typical of ranids that experience delayed maturity and relatively low annual adult mortality once they reach breeding age.

The transformation from a gill-breathing larva to a terrestrial juvenile represents a critical bottleneck in the species' life cycle. Free-swimming tadpoles feed on algae and detritus, building the energy reserves necessary for the dramatic body plan reorganization that characterizes amphibian metamorphosis. During the metamorphic climax, tail resorption and limb bud development proceed rapidly, and the recently metamorphosed froglet emerges onto land weighing only a fraction of its ultimate adult mass. The reproductive biology of the species is tightly linked to water temperature, as egg development and larval growth rates are highly sensitive to thermal conditions. In the laboratory, tadpoles reared at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] exhibit slower but more consistent growth than those exposed to fluctuating thermal regimes, and this stable temperature is used as a standard reference for comparing life-history traits across populations of Lithobates septentrionalis.

Breeding typically occurs in late spring at the margins of permanent lakes and ponds, where males establish calling territories to attract females. The reproductively active adult engages in amplexus, during which the female deposits her egg mass in shallow, well-oxygenated water. The gelatinous egg mass, often attached to submerged vegetation, contains several hundred to several thousand embryonated eggs, each surrounded by a protective jelly capsule. Predation on eggs and larvae by fish and aquatic insects is a major source of early mortality, favoring the production of large clutches as a compensatory life-history tactic. Despite the high fecundity, the condensed breeding window constrains total annual output, and the species' reliance on permanent water bodies, combined with its slow growth to maturity, renders it particularly vulnerable to habitat loss and wetland drainage.
